rationale:
Today's slate is 1 long-form, 3 Shorts and 1 carousel. The long-form is Lane A because nothing on the radar qualifies for Lane C or Lane B.

**Why Lane A.** The newest named next-gen result, the retatrutide sleep apnea trials in NEJM, came out Oct 20. That is outside Lane C's 48-hour window. Lane B is short one video this week, but the only fresh gray-market angle is the retatrutide Reddit study plus the CBS lab tests. Both ran as Shorts on 10-16 and 10-22, and the playbook bans a long-form on a topic covered as a Short in the last 14 days. So L1 is the playbook's top Lane A search phrase: tirzepatide side effects.

**L1.** It's an evergreen guide built from several sources: SURMOUNT-1 and SURPASS rates by arm against placebo, the FDA labels, the gut-motility mechanism and guideline-based comfort habits. It is not a single-trial deep dive. Every claim rests on settled primary sources, so it should pass fact-check, and it links to our live "How Long Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Take to Work?".

**Shorts.**
- **S1 (13:00 lead):** the fresh retatrutide sleep apnea result, with drug and condition in the title. Retatrutide Shorts have a median of 120 views, and the TRANSCEND-T2D-1 Short got 238.
- **S2:** an honest-uncertainty test, the format behind our best Instagram Reel (macular degeneration: 105 YouTube views, 160 reach). It uses ACOG's first GLP-1 pregnancy and breastfeeding guidance from Oct 23, so it adds a new dated fact rather than repeating the 10-15 carousel.
- **S3 (20:00 funnel):** a single-drug tirzepatide nausea question spun off from L1. It posts after L1 is live and names L1's exact title.

**Carousel.** C1 reuses only the verified text of the 10-22 macular degeneration Short. No new research, per the playbook.

**Mix.** 2 emerging (S1, S2), 2 evergreen with a timely hook (L1, S3) and 1 honest-uncertainty myth correction (C1).

**Variety.** Pillars: get-the-most ×2, research, is-it-for-you and myths. Body systems: gut ×2 (L1 and its spin-off), breathing during sleep, pregnancy and eyes. No "approved yet?", "beat" or how-to-list titles.

**Required on every piece:** the "Not personal advice" line, "talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you", no dosing, and no switching or stopping advice.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) side effects: which are common, why they happen, when they usually ease, what helps, and which signs to raise with a prescriber promptly
pieces.angle: Lane A (log 'lane: A' in metadata), series 'Life on GLP-1'. Hook (15 s or less): a one-line news hook (The Conversation, Oct 22, 2026, on GLP-1 nausea needing closer study), then the first answer: 'In the big trials, the most common side effects were stomach-related (nausea, diarrhoea, constipation, vomiting). Most were mild to moderate and happened mostly while the dose was being stepped up.' Use only the paper's wording for that timing. Chapters named as searched questions: (1) What are the most common tirzepatide side effects? Give SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022; adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks) rates for each dose arm vs placebo, with group sizes, copied exactly. Add one SURPASS line, labelled as type 2 diabetes. (2) Why does tirzepatide cause nausea? Slower stomach emptying and appetite signalling, citing the Neurogastroenterol Motil review and the label. (3) When do side effects get better? Only what the trials and label report, presented as averages, not predictions. (4) What helps with nausea and constipation? Habits recommended by the 2025 joint nutrition advisory and expert consensus: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping when comfortably full, fewer greasy meals, fluids (unless you've been told to limit fluids), and adding fibre gradually. Say 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'. (5) What else can happen? Injection-site reactions, plus discontinuation-for-side-effects rates vs placebo from the paper. (6) When to call your prescriber? Take the warning signs from the label exactly: severe or persistent belly pain (pancreatitis), gallbladder symptoms, dehydration with vomiting or diarrhoea, low blood sugar when combined with insulin or sulfonylureas, and the boxed thyroid warning in label wording. No dosing or titration talk, and never 'adjust your dose'. Re-hook every 45–75 s. The subscribe ask comes after the 'what helps' payoff. 'Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own.' End by naming 'How Long Does Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Take to Work?' as the video to watch next, then the full prescriber line. 8–12 min, 14:00 ET. Thumbnail (4 words or fewer): a relieved, labelled tummy character next to a tirzepatide pen, with text like 'Easier First Weeks'.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide for obstructive sleep apnea: TRIUMPH-1-OSA and TRIUMPH-2-OSA results in NEJM (Oct 20, 2026), adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and obesity or overweight, with and without type 2 diabetes, 80 weeks
pieces.angle: Retatrutide for sleep apnea, NEJM 20 Oct 2026: two Phase 3 trials (TRIUMPH-1-OSA without diabetes, TRIUMPH-2-OSA with type 2 diabetes), adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and BMI 27 or higher, 80 weeks, against placebo. Use the top dose arm ('top trial dose, 12 mg') against placebo for each trial: give the AHI change for both arms, group sizes and the paper's estimand, all taken only from NEJMoa2611477 and never from the TRIUMPH-1 obesity paper or from news sites. Then one line: 'smaller drops at lower doses'. Use one remission/mild-disease line with the paper's exact definition, or drop it if word count is tight. AHI = breathing pauses or shallow breaths per hour of sleep. GI side effects with the top-dose vs placebo rate for nausea only. Status: investigational, not approved anywhere; Lilly plans to file with the FDA in Q1 2027 (credit Lilly and the date of its statement). Context: tirzepatide (Zepbound) has been FDA-approved since 20 Dec 2024 for moderate-to-severe OSA with obesity; separate trials, not a head-to-head. 'If you use CPAP, don't stop or change it on your own; talk to your sleep clinician.' For approved options or a clinical trial, ask a prescriber. Never online sources. 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line, then 'follow for more'. 170 words or fewer.

pieces.why:
It's a new Phase 3 result for our best-performing Shorts name (retatrutide median 120; the type 2 diabetes result got 238), with low competition, and it adds a fact we haven't published before. | fact-check: Checked: NEJM, 'Retatrutide Once Weekly for Treatment of Obstructive Sleep Apnea' (TRIUMPH-1-OSA and TRIUMPH-2-OSA), published 20 Oct 2026 (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2611477), presented at Sleep Europe 2026. Population: adults with moderate-to-severe OSA and BMI 27 or higher, without or with type 2 diabetes. Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled. Lilly has said it plans to file in Q1 2027 (it's investigational; filing isn't approval). It fits the fresh-news lane.
Risks to fix:
(a) Secondary sources mix up AHI figures from the separate TRIUMPH-1 obesity paper (NEJMoa2604169, OSA subgroup: −22.9/−34.3/−31.7 vs −9.9) with the dedicated OSA trials. Take every number only from NEJMoa2611477 and check which trial each one belongs to.
(b) There were three dose arms in each trial, so per-arm results for both trials plus group sizes, remission, side effects and status won't fit in 170 words.
(c) The NEJM page returns 403 to automated fetch, so the scriptwriter must confirm the figures from the full text or the NEJM abstract page by hand. If any figure can't be confirmed, drop it rather than estimate.
The tirzepatide context line is fine: FDA approval for moderate-to-severe OSA with obesity on 20 Dec 2024, separate trials, no 'beat' framing.

pieces.topic: ACOG's first guidance on GLP-1 medicines (semaglutide, tirzepatide) in pregnancy planning and breastfeeding (Oct 23, 2026)
pieces.angle: Honest-uncertainty Short, credited 'ACOG Practice Advisory, Oct 23, 2026' and verified on acog.org. Open: 'On semaglutide or tirzepatide and thinking about pregnancy? It's a fair question, and the data is still limited.' ACOG advises clinicians to talk through the limited safety data and consider stopping these medicines 1–2 months before trying to conceive, as a plan made with your clinician. Why: they stay in the body a long time, and human pregnancy data is limited. Breastfeeding: if used, the baby's weight gain is closely monitored with the baby's clinician; ACOG advises against use when breastfeeding a preterm infant or newborn (use ACOG's exact wording). Calm context, labelled observational and credited to ACOG: early studies haven't shown a clear increase in major birth defects after accidental early exposure, which is not proof of safety. Tirzepatide can make birth control pills less reliable at times, so ask your prescriber about backup contraception. Unexpected pregnancy: tell your prescriber or OB-GYN right away, and they'll guide next steps. One GI line. 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line, then 'follow for more'. 170 words or fewer, no emoji.
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide or Tirzepatide and Pregnancy: What OB-GYNs Advise #shorts
pieces.why:
Fresh guidance from a major medical society (Oct 23) answers a high-intent question for a big part of our audience, and it tests the honest-uncertainty format behind our best Reel. It adds a new fact beyond the 10-15 carousel. | fact-check: Checked through Healio (23 Oct 2026). It's an ACOG Practice Advisory, written for clinicians. ACOG's wording: counsel patients about the lack of safety data and 'consider discontinuing GLP-1s 1–2 months before conception'. In lactation: shared decision-making, and 'closely monitor neonatal weight gain, in conjunction with the infant's clinician, if GLP-1s are used during breastfeeding'. It also advises against use in people breastfeeding preterm infants or neonates. On birth defects: 'early observational studies have not demonstrated a clear increase in major congenital malformations following inadvertent first-trimester exposure'. That is ACOG's line, so credit it to ACOG, not to 'consensus guidance'. The scriptwriter must confirm all of this on acog.org itself before scripting. It's a high-value safety topic for the audience.
Two fixes:
(1) Keep ACOG's verb 'consider stopping, with your clinician'. Never say 'ACOG says stop'.
(2) Remove 'don't stop or change your medicine on your own' from the unexpected-pregnancy line. The semaglutide and tirzepatide labels tell clinicians to discontinue when pregnancy is recognised, so that line could delay action. Use 'tell your prescriber or OB-GYN right away; they'll guide next steps, including diabetes care if you have it'.
Also add the tirzepatide label point that it can make birth control pills less reliable at times, and say 'ask your prescriber about backup contraception'. Don't give a schedule. Keep it calm, with no emoji and no 'Ozempic babies'.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide nausea: why slower stomach emptying causes it, when in the trials it was most common, and recommended comfort habits
pieces.angle: Same content, posted 10-25 at 20:00 ET (the day after L1 goes live), titled 'Tirzepatide Nausea: Why It Happens and What Helps #shorts'. Answer within 10 s: in SURMOUNT-1, nausea was the most common side effect on tirzepatide and happened mostly while the dose was being stepped up (the paper's wording), with per-arm vs placebo rates and group sizes. Present the timing as a trial average, not a prediction. Mechanism: food leaves the stomach more slowly. Two recommended habits: smaller meals eaten slowly; fewer greasy meals (and fluids unless you've been told to limit them). Red flag: severe or persistent belly pain or vomiting means contact your prescriber promptly. 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line. Spin-off of L1. Two problems:
(1) Scheduling. The playbook says spin-off Shorts run the day after their long-form, because a same-day Short on the same question may compete ('Not Working Yet?' got 62). Post it on 10-25 at 20:00 ET, after L1 is live.

Numbers: SURMOUNT-1 nausea by arm (5/10/15 mg vs placebo; n = 630/636/630/643; 72 weeks; adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes) must be copied exactly from the NEJM 2022 paper. Habits are 'recommended', not proven on the drug. Keep the fluids caveat. Red flag: severe or persistent belly pain, or vomiting that won't stop, means contact your prescriber promptly. No dosing talk. The L1 URL goes in description line 1 and the pinned comment, never a placeholder.
